Prove the conjunction by treating each `Iff` as an equivalence between two independently valid universal facts; there is no need to derive either side from the other.

- For binary products, use the defining property of `PreservesLimitPair.iso`. Its inverse transports the product cone on `(G X, G Y)` to the image under `G` of the product cone on `(X, Y)`. Compatibility with the second leg gives
  \[
  (\mathrm{PreservesLimitPair.iso}\,G\,X\,Y)^{-1}\;\gg\;G(\mathrm{snd})=\mathrm{snd}.
  \]
  This is a standard projection/naturality lemma, or follows immediately from uniqueness of morphisms into a product.

- For binary coproducts, use the comparison-isomorphism criterion: if `coprodComparison G X Y` is an isomorphism, then the image under `G` of the chosen coproduct cocone is colimiting. Hence `G` preserves that pair-shaped colimit.

- For the adjunction statement, the forward implication is composition: the left adjoint `F` preserves colimits, so if `H` preserves `J`-colimits, then `F ⋙ H` does. Conversely, fullness and faithfulness of the right adjoint `G` make the counit
  \[
  F G \cong \mathrm{Id}_D
  \]
  an isomorphism. Thus every diagram in `D` is, up to isomorphism, obtained by applying `F` to its image under `G`. Compute the latter diagram’s colimit in `C`, using `HasColimitsOfShape J C`, and transfer preservation from `F ⋙ H` across the counit isomorphism. Full faithfulness of `G` is the essential assumption here.

- For initial objects, apply the nullary version of the same comparison criterion: an invertible `initialComparison` says precisely that the image of the chosen initial object is initial, so the empty colimit is preserved.

After establishing these four standard facts, assemble the two `Iff`s by supplying the appropriate universal fact in each direction, ignoring the direction’s hypothesis, and then pair them with `And.intro`.
